q: An unexpected message urgently asks you to verify your password. What should you do?
options: Verify through an official, trusted channel
Forward your credentials to a colleague
why: Urgency + credential requests are classic phishing signs. Go to the official site yourself or call the helpdesk.

q: Which is the strongest warning sign of a phishing email?
options: Sender domain looks slightly different from the real one and demands payment today
It was sent on a Monday
why: Look-alike sender domains combined with urgent payment requests are high-risk signs.

q: Which password approach is generally safest?
options: A long unique passphrase per account stored in a password manager
why: Unique long passphrases limit the damage of reuse; a manager makes this practical.

q: Why enable MFA?
options: A stolen password alone is not enough to sign in
why: MFA adds a second factor. Phishing-resistant options like passkeys are even better.

q: A caller claims to be IT and asks for your MFA code. You should:
options: Refuse and report; IT never needs your code
why: Legitimate staff never need your one-time codes. Report the attempt.

q: Before entering a password on a site you should check:
options: That the domain is exactly the one you expect
why: A padlock only means encrypted traffic, not a trustworthy site. Check the domain.

q: Which practice best reduces ransomware impact?
options: Offline/immutable backups that are tested regularly
why: Tested backups let you recover without paying; patching and least privilege reduce the chance of infection.

q: Which is the best habit for sharing personal data?
options: Share only what is needed and review app permissions
why: Data minimisation reduces exposure if a service is breached.

q: On public Wi-Fi you should:
options: Avoid sensitive logins or use a trusted VPN/mobile data
why: Open networks can be monitored or spoofed; prefer trusted connections.

q: You clicked a suspicious link. What now?
why: Early reporting lets the security team contain issues quickly. Reporting is never punished in a good security culture.

q: An email has an unexpected attachment from an unknown sender. Best action?
options: Report it and do not open it
why: Unexpected attachments are a common delivery route; report instead of opening.

q: A message includes a QR code asking you to sign in. What is safest?
options: Navigate to the service yourself via its official app/site
why: QR codes hide the destination; go to the official site directly.

q: A 'CEO' emails asking for an urgent gift-card purchase. This is most likely:
why: Urgent payment requests from executives should be verified through a second channel.

q: What is a password manager mainly good for?
options: Creating and storing unique strong passwords
why: It lets you use a unique password everywhere without memorising them.

q: Why is password reuse risky?
options: One breach can unlock many accounts
why: Attackers try leaked credentials on other services (credential stuffing).

q: Which is the stronger secret?
why: Length and unpredictability beat clever substitutions.

q: Which MFA method is generally most phishing-resistant?
why: WebAuthn credentials are bound to the real site, so fake pages can't reuse them.

q: You get repeated MFA prompts you did not trigger. You should:
options: Deny them, change your password and report it
why: MFA-fatigue attempts mean your password may be exposed.

q: Strong password + MFA compared with password alone is:
why: A second factor blocks many account takeovers even if the password leaks.

q: A stranger asks to follow you into a secure door ('tailgating'). You should:
options: Politely ask them to badge in or contact security
why: Physical access should be authenticated for everyone.

q: Which is a pretexting red flag?
options: Request with a plausible story that bypasses normal process
why: Attackers invent stories to make you skip verification.

q: A pop-up says your device is infected and to call a number. You should:
options: Close the tab/browser and run your trusted security tool
why: Scareware relies on panic; close it and use trusted tools.

q: Safest place to download software:
options: The vendor's official site or store
why: Unofficial sources often bundle unwanted or harmful software.

q: Why keep backups offline or immutable?
options: So ransomware cannot encrypt or delete them
why: Backups reachable from the network can also be encrypted.

q: First step if you see files suddenly renamed/encrypted?
options: Disconnect from the network if advised and report immediately
why: Fast reporting limits spread; follow your incident procedure.

q: Which app permission request deserves a second look?
why: Permissions should match what the app needs to do.

q: Before posting online you should think about:
options: What the post reveals (location, routine, workplace)
why: Oversharing helps social-engineering and stalking.

q: Which is safer at a cafe?
options: Using mobile data or a trusted VPN for sensitive tasks
why: Open networks can be spoofed ('evil twin').

q: For home Wi-Fi you should:
why: Default credentials are widely known.

q: Why install OS updates on your phone?
why: Updates fix known flaws attackers target.

q: Best source of mobile apps:
why: Official stores add vetting; sideloading raises risk.

q: If your phone is lost, first:
options: Use remote lock/wipe and report it
why: Remote lock/wipe protects data; report to IT.

q: Who should you report a suspected phishing email to?
options: Your security/IT team via the official channel
why: Reports help protect others and improve detection.

q: A good incident report includes:
options: What happened, when, and what you did
why: Facts and timing help responders; certainty is not required.

q: Why report even if you're unsure?
options: Early reports prevent small issues becoming incidents
why: Speed matters more than being right.

q: Hovering over a link shows a different domain than the text. This suggests:
why: Mismatched link targets are a warning sign.

q: A 'vendor' asks you to change bank details by email. Best step?
options: Verify with a known phone number before changing anything
why: Out-of-band verification stops payment-redirection fraud.

q: A padlock in the address bar means:
options: The site is safe to enter passwords
why: Encryption doesn't prove the site is honest.

q: Why use different emails/aliases for different services?
why: Compartmentalising reduces linkage.

q: Which control helps most by limiting damage once an account is compromised?
why: Users and services should only have access they need.
